title: Space resilience: access, threats and investment
label: 16 November 2026 · Space resilience
summary: The committee examined how heavily the UK’s armed forces and economy depend on space services, and how vulnerable those services are to attack or to being switched off by a provider. The witnesses agreed that losing access would not make Britain unable to fight, but would make its forces far less effective. They differed on whether national security systems should be bought only from allies, while stressing the need for reliable access, stronger UK and European capabilities, clearer government leadership and steady investment.

chapters.title: How much the military depends on space
chapters.takeaway: Space services underpin military communications, tracking and movement, and losing them would sharply reduce the armed forces’ effectiveness.

turns.speaker: Helen Maguire
turns.text: Modern forces rely heavily on space for things like tracking targets and warning of missile attacks. What dependence worries you most?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: There are several. Military satellite communications are a major concern: at the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, an attack on Viasat’s satellite internet disrupted Ukrainian military communications and command.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: There have also been cases where access to commercial satellite imagery was suspended, and where limits were placed on Starshield, a military satellite communications service. Those events show that access can be disrupted or restricted, including by a provider.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Space, air, land and sea operations are connected. Without space services, forces lose information about what is happening, reliable navigation and timing, and the ability to communicate and share data. They can still fight, but not as effectively.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: We also need to be able to launch replacements. It’s not enough to rely on today’s satellite services if we can’t replenish them when they’re lost or disrupted.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: If British forces lost access to their own or American space services, how prepared would they be?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: They could still fight using basics such as maps and compasses, but they wouldn’t be efficient or effective. Around 3,000 systems in an Army brigade rely on space services. If those services weren’t assured, we’d need far more equipment and investment to make up the difference.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Would more automated and connected forces become even more vulnerable if space services were disrupted, or if an ally switched them off?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Yes. We’re putting more military capability onto networks that depend on space. We should ask both whether we can stop an adversary from attacking those services and whether we can withstand an attack and keep providing what the armed forces need.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Russia destroyed one of its own satellites three months before invading Ukraine, demonstrating a capability. We have to consider whether we can discourage such actions and, if that fails, absorb the first blow and continue operating.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: So you can’t confidently say that we’re ready?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: No, I can’t give you a clear yes.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Would the defence investment plan close the gap?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: The strategy sets out what we want to achieve, and the plan identifies resources. My concern is whether we can put the changes in place fast enough to keep pace with a rapidly growing threat.

chapters.title: Reliable access and trusted partners
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses argued for dependable access to space services, but differed on how far the UK should limit purchases to allied suppliers.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: The future force will be more connected and automated, with long-range precision attacks relying on a digital targeting network. Losing space services wouldn’t stop it working overnight, but it would gradually reduce its range, accuracy, speed, awareness and ability to coordinate.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Does that mean the strategy to modernise the forces has a single point of failure in its reliance on space?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: I wouldn’t put it quite that way, but the strategy’s aim of making the forces as effective as possible depends heavily on space—perhaps more than people realise.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: We should discuss how to guarantee secure access, rather than assume we can make every part of the supply chain British. For example, the UK could keep the design authority for systems so it can update software without asking another country for permission.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: We could also build more local manufacturing and intellectual property capability so we can replace or reproduce equipment after an attack. We’ll still depend on the US and other allies for years; simply removing US systems from our defence arrangements wouldn’t work in the near term.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Do we also rely on suppliers outside our close group of allies?

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: I can’t give a complete account, but chips, semiconductors and rare-earth materials for important systems come from countries that aren’t allies. We need to trace those supply chains to understand the risks.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: We need a more careful distinction: some capabilities may need to be under British control; others need guaranteed access; and some can come from trusted partners or commercial suppliers. Working with allies such as Japan could also stretch a limited UK budget, though that brings its own dependencies.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Can technology prevent jamming and spoofing, or is this mainly a matter of investing enough?

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: There isn’t one fix. Resilience can come from several sources, including alternatives on the ground as well as different satellite services. The UK is exploring ground-based navigation and working with Eutelsat OneWeb to widen the choice of providers.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Having several options makes it less likely that an opponent can disable everything with one action. It may also make an attack less attractive, since damage in space can create consequences for everyone.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: Should the Government buy national security systems only from allies?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: No. We need a wider range of suppliers, but we shouldn’t cut ourselves off from our closest allies.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Yes. I think national security assets should be bought only from allies.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: I agree with Michelle.

chapters.title: What government and industry should do
chapters.takeaway: Industry wants predictable government demand and clearer leadership, with launch and space-protection capabilities among the investment priorities.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: What does industry need from government to address these risks?

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: The defence investment plan’s focus on protecting and controlling space is a good direction. Government is becoming an important customer, so it should build a long-term relationship with companies.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Grants for research and development have a role, but over time government should buy more working capabilities, giving companies a dependable market. A clear year-by-year spending pipeline would help firms decide to invest in the UK.

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: The UK should also better support companies trying to sell space and defence products abroad. Overseas customers can provide a market beyond what the UK can offer by itself.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: Which areas should receive public investment?

turns.speaker: Nathan Mathiot
turns.text: Launch capability is a priority. The UK and Europe rely too much on existing launch capacity, including SpaceX, and need to strengthen their own ability to send satellites into space.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: The most useful thing government can provide is a clear plan and a reliable stream of contracts. ISAM—repairing, assembling and manufacturing things in orbit—is also an area where the UK could build on existing strengths.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Government needs to make clear who is responsible for space. Several ministers have been associated with the UK space strategy, and it isn’t clear who is ultimately in charge.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Buying and developing equipment also needs to move faster. The plans point to a clear gap in space control—the ability to protect our own use of space and limit an opponent’s. That is closely connected to the kind of in-orbit capability Michelle described.

chapters.title: Threats and public understanding
chapters.takeaway: Space threats range from signal disruption to weapons that can destroy satellites, while the witnesses said both the public and government need to take space’s importance more seriously.

turns.speaker: Lord Godson
turns.text: What are the main threats to space systems, including from China, and how well do government and the public understand them? Should Space Command have greater status?

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Threats range from reversible interference with signals to nuclear explosions in orbit. They also include satellites that can grapple with other satellites and missiles launched from Earth to destroy them. These are real capabilities, not science fiction.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: China has more sophisticated space capabilities and depends on space more than Russia does. I see China as more predictable, while Russia has acted in ways I wouldn’t expect from a rational leadership. Together, their ability to disrupt space has grown substantially since 2021.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Space gets more attention when senior military leaders explain what it means in practice. For example, a commander might say that ships can’t leave port without being seen by an opponent’s satellites.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: Space Command should grow, but the wider defence organisation also needs to treat space and cyber as part of military operations. The defence budget hasn’t grown simply because the military now has five operating areas instead of three.

turns.speaker: Major General Paul Tedman
turns.text: We’ve run exercises showing Ministers and members of the public what a day without space services might look like. One estimate is that losing the timing signal alone could cost the UK economy £1 billion a day.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: A recent UK survey found that 21% of people first associated space with aliens, while only 8% thought of communications and connectivity. That shows how much public understanding still needs to improve.

turns.speaker: Dr Michelle Howard
turns.text: Astronauts and rocket launches attract attention, so we can use that interest to explain how space supports areas such as transport, investment and logistics.
